name: John Maynard Keynes
role: British economist, Liberal supporter and Bretton Woods negotiator (1883-1946)
summary: Keynes described himself as a liberal who rejected both laissez-faire and doctrinaire state socialism, wanting central control of money, credit and investment to secure full employment inside a market economy. He favoured graduated taxation, the 'euthanasia of the rentier', pacifism and arbitration, and opposed Bolshevism and totalitarian rule while stressing personal liberty and variety.

abolish-central-banks.rationale: He wants the currency and credit controlled deliberately by a central institution.

abolish-income-tax.rationale: He treats income tax and surtax as the instruments by which disparities of wealth have been reduced and wants them used further.

arbitrator-settles-disputes.rationale: He supports setting an example 'in the direction of Arbitration and of Disarmament' and wants breaches of the reparation settlement referred to the League.

arms-reduction.rationale: He favours giving a good example in arbitration and disarmament even at the risk of being weak.

automate-paid-work.rationale: He welcomes technical progress that lets people work far less, proposing a fifteen-hour week.

avoid-deficit-stimulus.rationale: He argued repeatedly that governments should borrow to finance capital works in a slump and attacked budget cuts and the Sinking Fund as deflationary.

capital-controls.rationale: He told the Lords that each member government under the Bretton Woods plan has 'the explicit right to control all capital movements', and in 1933 urged that finance be primarily national.

capitalism-adapts.rationale: He defends enlarged government functions as the only practicable means of avoiding the destruction of existing economic forms and says capitalism wisely managed can be made more efficient than any alternative in sight.

capitalism-causes-war.rationale: He names the competitive struggle for markets under laissez-faire and the gold standard as an economic cause of war, but argues full-employment policy at home would remove that motive.

capitalism-progressive.rationale: In 'Economic Possibilities' he credits the accumulation of capital and technical progress with bringing the economic problem within sight of solution within a hundred years.

central-bank-independence.rationale: He argued in 1923 for a presumption in favour of stable internal prices, and described the Bank of England as a semi-autonomous body, but the General Theory has the State fixing the rate of interest and he ranked full employment above price stability later.

central-planning.rationale: He writes that the advantage of decentralised decisions and individual responsibility is greater than the nineteenth century supposed and that centralising decisions would not avoid errors of foresight.

class-collaboration.rationale: He rejects lip-service to 'the beauties of the class war' and wants a party disinterested between classes, though he says the class war would find him on the bourgeois side.

collective-defense.rationale: He opposes pledging British forces in advance to defend an ally, calling a duty to join every future western European war unnecessary.

cut-consumption-tax.rationale: In 1931 he complained that tea, sugar and a tariff were left untapped as revenue sources while teachers were cut.

decent-living-guarantee.rationale: In 1931 he attacked the Economy Committee's cuts to the dole and public pay as deflationary and unjust, though he also wanted the grave abuses of the dole reformed; he gives no dependency argument.

decide-locally.rationale: He urges decentralising and devolving wherever possible, placing the ideal unit of control between the individual and the modern State, though in semi-autonomous bodies rather than strictly local ones.

dictatorship-of-proletariat.rationale: He rejects Bolshevism's creed of persecution and revolutionary tactics and says Red revolution would throw a Western population into a pit of poverty and death.

disputed-territory-plebiscite.rationale: In his proposed treaty revision he keeps the Upper Silesia plebiscite and says the inhabitants' wishes should be regarded.

economic-freedom.rationale: He calls economic individualism, purged of its abuses, the best safeguard of personal liberty.

economic-self-sufficiency.rationale: In 1945 he spoke against bilateral barter and 'separate economic blocs', and in 1933 he treated national self-sufficiency only as a means 'not as an ideal in itself'.

empower-international-orgs.rationale: In 1919 he hoped the League might be transformed into a powerful instrument of peace, and in 1945 he hoped Anglo-American arrangements lead to institutions that are 'the first step towards something more comprehensive'.

encourage-eccentricity.rationale: He prizes tolerance, variety and independence and wants 'unhindered opportunity to the exceptional and to the aspiring'; the General Theory says variety of life is the highest loss in a homogeneous state.

end-foreign-alliances.rationale: He says 'I am against Pacts' and calls pledging British forces to defend Germany against France foolish.

equal-outcomes.rationale: He holds that there is social and psychological justification for significant inequalities of income and wealth, though not for such large ones.

experts-over-public.rationale: He expects the new duties of government to be given to semi-independent expert corporations since ministers and Parliament will be unserviceable, but keeps Parliament sovereign in the last resort.

flat-income-tax.rationale: He praises direct taxation through income tax, surtax and death duties as having reduced disparities and wishes the process carried further.

four-day-week.rationale: He suggests three-hour shifts or a fifteen-hour week to share what work remains as widely as possible.

free-trade.rationale: In 1925 he said he believed in free trade because in the long run and in general it is technically sound; by 1931-33 he accepted a revenue tariff and doubted its universal claims, and in 1945 he again backed multilateral trade.

free-trade-promotes-peace.rationale: He wrote in 1933 that more self-sufficiency than in 1914 may serve peace rather than otherwise and that the old internationalism was not particularly successful in avoiding war, yet in 1919 proposed a Free Trade Union under the League and in 1945 backed multilateral trade.

gradual-change.rationale: He says the next step must come from thought, 'not from political agitation or premature experiments', and prefers gradual reform.

income-for-work-not-ownership.rationale: He calls for the 'euthanasia of the rentier' and the functionless investor, since interest rewards no genuine sacrifice, while paying financiers and entrepreneurs reasonable rewards for skill and judgement.

legalize-drugs.rationale: He thinks prohibiting spirits and bookmakers would do good yet asks how far humanity may be allowed escape, such as 'permitted Saturnalia', so his view is mixed.

limit-population.rationale: He says each country needs a considered policy on population, which may mean larger or smaller numbers, and names control of population a condition of economic bliss.

markets-allocate-better.rationale: In The General Theory ch. 24 he holds that once central controls secure full employment, private self-interest can decide what is produced and in what proportions, and that centralising decisions would not avoid errors of allocation.

material-conditions-drive-history.rationale: He credits secular economic causes such as population growth for great events, but also says ideas rather than vested interests rule the world.

money-backed-by-precious-metals.rationale: He told the Lords that the Bretton Woods plan is 'the exact opposite' of the gold standard, and had earlier called gold a 'barbarous relic'.

moral-incentives.rationale: He sympathises with Russian Communism's attempt to demote the money motive yet says capitalism depends on it and calls the money-motive useful.

nation-first.rationale: He argued in 1933 that finance should be primarily national and self-sufficiency affordable, yet in 1944-45 he negotiated Bretton Woods as a framework of cooperation that kept domestic policy under national control.

national-self-determination.rationale: He faults the Treaty for breaching Wilson's self-determination in barring German-Austria's union with Germany, but also deplores the new 'greedy, jealous, immature' nationalist states carved from the empires.

neither-capitalism-nor-communism.rationale: He rejects laissez-faire, doctrinaire State Socialism and Communism alike, and says no party has the right aims and methods and a new set of convictions is needed.

night-watchman-state.rationale: He sets government an 'Agenda' of tasks beyond defence and justice, such as controlling credit and investment, and says laissez-faire cannot be settled on principle.

no-central-bank.rationale: He argues that a central institution must control currency and credit, and that a managed currency cannot be avoided in a world of paper money and bank credit.

one-party-rule.rationale: He lists Fascism and Bolshevism as the abuses of the new age in government and writes that authoritarian state systems solve unemployment at the expense of efficiency and freedom.

parliament-supreme.rationale: He wants semi-autonomous public bodies subject 'in the last resort to the sovereignty of the democracy expressed through Parliament'.

price-stability-first.rationale: In 1923 he favoured stability of prices over stability of exchange, but from the 1930s his stated aim was full employment, so the sources point both ways.

property-fundamental.rationale: He states that it is not true that individuals possess a prescriptive 'natural liberty' in economic activity and that no compact confers perpetual rights on those who have or acquire.

public-ownership.rationale: In 'The End of Laissez-faire' he says big public-utility undertakings still need to be semi-socialised, preferably as semi-autonomous public corporations, while calling nationalisation of the railways a question of little importance.

regulate-corporations.rationale: He wants society to exercise directive intelligence over private business, with legally required publicity of business facts and central control of credit, while leaving private initiative unhindered.

results-over-ideology.rationale: He says issues cannot be settled on abstract grounds but must be handled on their merits in detail, and rejects both laissez-faire and doctrinaire State Socialism as obsolete creeds.

state-directs-investment.rationale: He calls for a 'somewhat comprehensive socialisation of investment' and for coordinated judgement on the scale and channels of national saving rather than leaving them to private profit.

state-harmful.rationale: He says government must take on many duties it has avoided and calls its Agenda the thing individuals do not do at all.

suppress-opposition.rationale: He condemns Soviet persecution of resisters and spy networks as detestable and prizes tolerance and independence.

tariffs-protect-industry.rationale: His 1931 proposal was a flat revenue tariff with 'no discriminating protective taxes', and the General Theory grants mercantilism a kernel of truth, while in 1925 he still held free trade sound and in 1944-45 opposed discriminatory practices.

tax-holding-cash.rationale: He calls Gesell's stamped money, which taxes holding currency, 'sound' in idea and possibly practicable on a modest scale.

tax-inheritance.rationale: The General Theory ch. 24 defends heavy death duties as raising consumption without harming capital growth, and notes that justifications for inequality of income do not apply equally to inheritance.

tax-the-wealthy.rationale: The General Theory ch. 24 argues that growth does not depend on the savings of the rich, so one chief justification for great inequality is removed, and that some inequality is justified but not 'such large disparities as exist to-day'.

taxation-theft.rationale: He treats taxation as a legitimate instrument for guiding the propensity to consume and reducing inequality.

total-state.rationale: He calls the loss of variety in the 'homogeneous or totalitarian state' the greatest of all losses and defends individualism as the safeguard of personal choice.

totalitarianisms-equivalent.rationale: He groups Fascism on one side and Bolshevism on the other as the abuses of the stabilisation era, though he does not call them equivalent.

trade-surplus.rationale: The General Theory ch. 24 says that once nations secure full employment at home there is no motive to force wares on others to build a favourable trade balance; Bretton Woods put adjustment duties on creditor countries.

unions-good.rationale: He calls trade unionists 'once the oppressed, now the tyrants' whose sectional claims must be opposed, yet defends the miners against wage cuts and backs unions' resistance to being made victims of economic forces.

work-centre-of-life.rationale: In 'Economic Possibilities' he looks to a future when the economic problem is solved and people spend three hours a day or less at work, finding purpose elsewhere.

notes: Texts searched: Essays in Persuasion, General Theory, Economic Consequences of the Peace, Means to Prosperity, National Self-Sufficiency and three Lords speeches (1944-45). Themes searched: economy, taxation, trade, money, government form, peace and alliances, sex and drugs, population, technology. Eugenics Society roles were found but his own position on state action is not stated, so those statements stay null. Positions on tariffs and free trade shift between 1925, 1931-33 and 1944-45 and are recorded as mixed. O'Donnell (s9) reports continuity in his political philosophy over time.
